The author is overwhelmed caring for her mom with Alzheimer's.

Courtesy of the author

  • I spend hours each week coordinating my mother's care.
  • Daily calls, paperwork, and emergencies have become part of my routine.
  • Caregiving has left little room to process my own grief.

When my mother was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease two-and-a-half years ago, it soon became apparent that she would need 24-hour care.

I work full-time and live in a small apartment with two kids, so caring for her myself or having her move in with me was not an option. Thankfully (after nine months and tons of red tape), I was able to get her into a Medicaid program and arrange full-time in-home care for her.

What I didn't expect was that caring for her would still be a full-time job. Don't get me wrong. I love my mother and want to help her. Her condition is heartbreaking, and I'm extremely grateful that she has people with her to manage her moment-by-moment care needs, like cooking, cleaning, grooming, medication reminders, and making sure she stays safe.

Still, I never expected how much work caregiving for an elderly parent would be, even if I'm not providing direct 24/7 care.

My mom is reliant on me

My mother is extremely reliant on me emotionally. She can still use her phone, so I get about 20 to 30 texts and about one to 10 phone calls from her daily.

Each time her aide gives her medication, she texts me to ask what it's called. She asks me multiple times a day when I will see her next, even after I answer her. It's endless repeated questions, confusion, and fears. I can't respond to everything, but I have to respond sometimes, and it's a constant interruption to my day.

I live five minutes away from her, so anytime she needs something, it falls on my husband or me. She can no longer shop or run errands and often needs help with this or that around her house. We are there multiple times a week helping her. She tends to lose things, break things, or cause other problems at home that require outside support. I also make it a practice to spend one afternoon a week with her just spending time together.

I'm always on the phone, figuring out paperwork

Then, there's the health insurance paperwork and phone calls, doctor phone calls, calls with caregivers, calls with other family members, etc. Not a day goes by that I'm not on the phone with someone or an organization that helps provide her care.

I also take my mother to every doctor's appointment she has, which can be quite frequent. I manage her medication, which includes renewals, pharmacy pick-ups, and filling her medication trays weekly for her aides. I also manage her finances and pay all bills.

On top of all this, there's almost always some emergency each week. Last week, my mother locked two different doors in her apartment from the inside, making the rooms inaccessible, and we had to call an emergency handyman to get them opened. We then had to go out and buy new doorknobs and figure out how to temporarily disable the remaining doorknobs in her house so she wouldn't lock them, too.

I'm on the phone with her aides, my other family members, and her doctors to discuss how to handle things.

I grieve for who my mom once was

The whole thing is just so much to manage, and so stressful, too. I spend many sleepless nights wondering how I'm going to do all the things I need to do for her, and how I can possibly do it all for the next few years, as she continues to live with her condition. She is in her late 70s, so it may still be another few years before she lives with this condition. Alzheimer's is progressive and incurable, and while the caregiving tasks will evolve, they will continue to be here for the rest of her life.

While I grieve for my mother and what her life has become, sometimes I feel like I have little time to feel sadness. The kind of care I provide for her is so relentless and so stressful that there is almost no time for me to even consider my own feelings about what's happening to her. When do I get to say goodbye if I'm knee-deep in the daily tasks that are necessary to keep her safe, all while she deteriorates before my eyes?

I know that one day I'll look back at this time and remember all the little moments we had together — the way I held her hand as we took a walk through her neighborhood, the contented sighs from her on the other end of the phone while I reassured her again that I would see her soon. I know she would appreciate all the tasks I do for her if she understood what was going on around her. I know that each thing I do is an act of love.

But I am drowning in these caregiving tasks, and sometimes wonder how I'm going to make it through the next bunch of years with my mental health intact.

items.title: After starting the tokenmaxxing panic, Uber's CTO is back with a very different AI story
items.summary: Uber CTO Praveen Neppalli Naga Uber A version of this story originally appeared in the BI Tech Memo newsletter. Sign up for the weekly BI Tech Memo newsletter here . Remember the executive who sparked the tokenmaxxing panic earlier this year after saying Uber had already blown through its 2026 budget for Anthropic's Claude Code? He's back with a more interesting lesson about AI. Uber CTO Praveen Neppalli Naga says the company has started sending its best AI engineers into departments like finance, legal, marketing, customer support, HR, and procurement to study how people actually work before building AI tools with them. He called these two-week teams "Agentic Pods." Engineers spend the first few days shadowing employees, learning every step of a workflow, then quickly build and test software to improve it. The results are striking. One financial planning process dropped from 15 hours to 30 minutes. Financial reports fell from two days to 10 minutes. Marketing quality checks shrank from two weeks to less than an hour. Naga said the biggest gains rarely come from speeding up one task. They come from redesigning an entire workflow around AI, eliminating unnecessary approvals, replacing old software, and helping people make decisions faster. You can see this at work here , too. Several tech executives compared the approach to Silicon Valley's fast-growing "forward-deployed engineer" role. The twist? Instead of sending these AI experts to customers, Uber is deploying them inside its own business to find the next wave of productivity gains. Peter Wilczynski, chief product officer at Vantortech, jokingly dubbed the role the " Rearward Deployed Engineer ," describing engineers embedded deep inside corporate operations to redesign entire workflows around AI rather than simply speeding up individual tasks. items.title: I built my tiny home from scratch for under $50,000. Doing it all myself was hard, but the money I'm saving is worth it.
items.summary: Margo Fairchild in front of her Virginia tiny home. Courtesy of Margo Fairchild In 2020, Margo Fairchild built a tiny home on her own with no prior experience. Fairchild spent countless hours and almost all her paychecks to build the 240-square-foot home. It took 15 months and $43,779 to build the home, but the freedom she has is priceless, she said. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Margo Fairchild, 34, who built a 240-square-foot tiny home in Virginia on her own in 2020. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. I grew up watching my dad work with his hands, mostly on cars, and I picked up a bit of resourcefulness and that get-it-done attitude from him. So, when I decided I wanted to live in a tiny home , it never really crossed my mind to have someone else build it for me. Maybe that was partly because of the expense, but after spending a few years researching and studying building science, I felt like I could take it on myself. I started construction in 2020 and took 15 months to build my 240-square-foot tiny home. It wasn't like an HGTV show where you see the finished reveal 20 minutes later. I was in the weeds, working on it every single day. The hardest part of the project was finding the grit to keep going while working 14- to 18-hour days, often after my regular job and on weekends. It was a huge mental burden. I would ask myself, "Can I really do this?" and then just keep pushing forward. Nearly all of my time and money were spent on construction My mom has a small piece of land — less than an acre. We agreed that I could build my home on her property and move in with her while it was under construction. In exchange, I gave her a little money for rent. I used my savings to pay for the project. Basically, any paycheck I had during that time went toward construction. Almost immediately, my budget flew out the window. Aside from the plumbing, Fairchild built the entire home herself. Courtest of Margo Fairchild One of my biggest expenses was purchasing the shell, which forms the home's basic structure. It didn't come with a ceiling, skylight, insulation, or any additional structural framing, so I had to add all of that myself. I learned as I went, and there was a lot of trial and error. I often turned to "YouTube University." I also started an Instagram page, and architects and builders from places as far away as Holland and Portland would reach out and offer advice whenever I had a question. I was building during the pandemic and couldn't have people come out to help, so it was nice to feel like I had a community of people to bounce ideas off of. Fairchild on the roof of the tiny home. Courtesy of Margo Fairchild The only work I hired out during the project was the plumbing. I hired someone who wasn't very reputable, which was definitely a big mistake. They connected my system to my mom's house, which uses a septic tank, and the entire setup failed. Wastewater from both homes flooded my mom's crawlspace. I had to pay another company to fix it, and in the end, I had to put about $7,000 to $8,000 on a credit card. But at that point, I didn't care. I had good credit and knew I could use my credit card if needed. Altogether, I ended up spending $43,779 to build the home — nearly double what I had expected. My home is small, but it meets all my needs I moved into my home in 2022, and I was so excited. I was 29 and single at the time, and living with my mom was just not it. My tiny home is basically a studio. It has one bedroom and one bathroom with a bathtub. My queen-size bed is lofted above the dining booth. It's really tiny. I recently got a dog, and she's under my feet all the time. Still, it's incredibly freeing to turn up my music, open the door, and let my dog run around in the fenced-in yard. It's nice to wake up, look around and say, "Hey, I did that." Fairchild's bedroom, dining area, and her sitting with her dog. Sage Roddy/Tiny Home Tours I don't feel like I had to give up too much when I downsized from a normal-sized home to a tiny home. It was actually pretty therapeutic to start with a clean slate. I left some of my things with my former partner and rent a storage unit where I store the rest. I also keep my winter clothes in a closet at my mom's house. Of course, there are drawbacks to living in a tiny home , like how quickly a small space gets cluttered. You definitely have to keep it tidy so you don't trip over something and break your neck. I would say the biggest drawback, though, is giving up the extra space for an office or just somewhere to tinker inside my home. But other than those things, I think my tiny home meets my needs. My tiny home is helping me save for retirement I pay my mom $500 a month to live on her property. Compared with the $2,000 to $3,000 I might pay elsewhere, the savings have allowed me to put more money toward retirement. The home has also created other sources of income. I documented the construction process on social media and monetized the content. Within two years, that income covered the cost of building the home. As my following grew, it also led to more opportunities in the design world, including becoming a co-host of HGTV's "Worst Yard on the Block." I've seen tiny homes becoming more popular, especially with young people. I think it's because, for many of us, our salaries just aren't comparable to what our parents — or even Gen Xers and boomers — were making relative to the cost of a house. I also think a lot of younger people value experiences . Instead of spending all their money on rent or a mortgage, they want to travel, and the expense and responsibility of maintaining a home can limit that freedom a bit. Margo Fairchild built a 240-square-foot tiny home by herself. Sage Roddy/Tiny Home Tours My advice to anyone who wants to build a tiny home is to find a support system. It doesn't have to be family or friends. Look for online forums or communities where you can turn on the difficult days —the ones when you're asking yourself, "What am I doing? Who do I think I am to believe I can do this?" Hearing from someone who has been in that position and can say, "I've done this. You can get through it," makes a huge difference. Despite the challenges, I would build my tiny home all over again. It was one of the hardest things I've ever done, but it was also one of the most rewarding. items.summary_html:
Margo Fairchild in front of her Virginia tiny home.

Courtesy of Margo Fairchild

  • In 2020, Margo Fairchild built a tiny home on her own with no prior experience.
  • Fairchild spent countless hours and almost all her paychecks to build the 240-square-foot home.
  • It took 15 months and $43,779 to build the home, but the freedom she has is priceless, she said.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Margo Fairchild, 34, who built a 240-square-foot tiny home in Virginia on her own in 2020. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

I grew up watching my dad work with his hands, mostly on cars, and I picked up a bit of resourcefulness and that get-it-done attitude from him.

So, when I decided I wanted to live in a tiny home, it never really crossed my mind to have someone else build it for me. Maybe that was partly because of the expense, but after spending a few years researching and studying building science, I felt like I could take it on myself.

I started construction in 2020 and took 15 months to build my 240-square-foot tiny home. It wasn't like an HGTV show where you see the finished reveal 20 minutes later. I was in the weeds, working on it every single day.

The hardest part of the project was finding the grit to keep going while working 14- to 18-hour days, often after my regular job and on weekends. It was a huge mental burden.

I would ask myself, "Can I really do this?" and then just keep pushing forward.

Nearly all of my time and money were spent on construction

My mom has a small piece of land — less than an acre. We agreed that I could build my home on her property and move in with her while it was under construction. In exchange, I gave her a little money for rent.

I used my savings to pay for the project. Basically, any paycheck I had during that time went toward construction.

Almost immediately, my budget flew out the window.

Aside from the plumbing, Fairchild built the entire home herself.

Courtest of Margo Fairchild

One of my biggest expenses was purchasing the shell, which forms the home's basic structure. It didn't come with a ceiling, skylight, insulation, or any additional structural framing, so I had to add all of that myself.

I learned as I went, and there was a lot of trial and error. I often turned to "YouTube University." I also started an Instagram page, and architects and builders from places as far away as Holland and Portland would reach out and offer advice whenever I had a question.

I was building during the pandemic and couldn't have people come out to help, so it was nice to feel like I had a community of people to bounce ideas off of.

Fairchild on the roof of the tiny home.

Courtesy of Margo Fairchild

The only work I hired out during the project was the plumbing. I hired someone who wasn't very reputable, which was definitely a big mistake. They connected my system to my mom's house, which uses a septic tank, and the entire setup failed. Wastewater from both homes flooded my mom's crawlspace.

I had to pay another company to fix it, and in the end, I had to put about $7,000 to $8,000 on a credit card. But at that point, I didn't care. I had good credit and knew I could use my credit card if needed.

Altogether, I ended up spending $43,779 to build the home — nearly double what I had expected.

My home is small, but it meets all my needs

I moved into my home in 2022, and I was so excited. I was 29 and single at the time, and living with my mom was just not it.

My tiny home is basically a studio. It has one bedroom and one bathroom with a bathtub. My queen-size bed is lofted above the dining booth. It's really tiny. I recently got a dog, and she's under my feet all the time.

Still, it's incredibly freeing to turn up my music, open the door, and let my dog run around in the fenced-in yard. It's nice to wake up, look around and say, "Hey, I did that."

Fairchild's bedroom, dining area, and her sitting with her dog.

Sage Roddy/Tiny Home Tours

I don't feel like I had to give up too much when I downsized from a normal-sized home to a tiny home. It was actually pretty therapeutic to start with a clean slate.

I left some of my things with my former partner and rent a storage unit where I store the rest. I also keep my winter clothes in a closet at my mom's house.

Of course, there are drawbacks to living in a tiny home, like how quickly a small space gets cluttered. You definitely have to keep it tidy so you don't trip over something and break your neck.

I would say the biggest drawback, though, is giving up the extra space for an office or just somewhere to tinker inside my home. But other than those things, I think my tiny home meets my needs.

My tiny home is helping me save for retirement

I pay my mom $500 a month to live on her property. Compared with the $2,000 to $3,000 I might pay elsewhere, the savings have allowed me to put more money toward retirement.

The home has also created other sources of income. I documented the construction process on social media and monetized the content. Within two years, that income covered the cost of building the home.

As my following grew, it also led to more opportunities in the design world, including becoming a co-host of HGTV's "Worst Yard on the Block."

I've seen tiny homes becoming more popular, especially with young people.

I think it's because, for many of us, our salaries just aren't comparable to what our parents — or even Gen Xers and boomers — were making relative to the cost of a house.

I also think a lot of younger people value experiences. Instead of spending all their money on rent or a mortgage, they want to travel, and the expense and responsibility of maintaining a home can limit that freedom a bit.

Margo Fairchild built a 240-square-foot tiny home by herself.

Sage Roddy/Tiny Home Tours

My advice to anyone who wants to build a tiny home is to find a support system.

It doesn't have to be family or friends. Look for online forums or communities where you can turn on the difficult days —the ones when you're asking yourself, "What am I doing? Who do I think I am to believe I can do this?"

Hearing from someone who has been in that position and can say, "I've done this. You can get through it," makes a huge difference.

Despite the challenges, I would build my tiny home all over again. It was one of the hardest things I've ever done, but it was also one of the most rewarding.

items.title: Latest open artifacts (#23): Laguna S2.1, Inkling, & Kimi K3 show the utility of open models on the Pareto frontier
items.summary: Consolidation has been one of the paths that many astute observers predicted for the near-future of labs training models. It was labelled as inevitable, as training costs are increasing by orders of magnitude every year. Yet, as someone who in 2024 would’ve predicted consolidation really picking up come 2026 or 2027, where are we? We’re at a place where more companies are training strong models — easily investing hundreds of millions to billions of dollars in the total effort still — and an increasing number of organizations are releasing these models openly. The demand for tokens is incredibly high, and likely to increase as models get more efficient and unlock more possible use cases. All of these labs we thought would need to consolidate are realizing that building token machines is a likely path to value, and more companies will identify that source of value over time. The prime example is Thinking Machines — when they announced their company in February 2025, very few people would’ve put them in the bucket of an open models company, myself included. Now their open model finetuning service is making hundreds of millions in revenue per year and they’re releasing the best open-weight models built in the U.S.A. — ahead of the early leaders in NVIDIA with Nemotron and Arcee’s Trilogy. Share On the other side of the ecosystem is the sustained pace from the Chinese labs, with newer entrants like Xiaomi still accumulating mindshare in the broader AI economy. Having predicted consolidation for a long time, it now seems like a safer bet is to predict continued adoption, and try to imagine the role that open models play there. How much can revenue-share licenses like Kimi K3 stick? How much market share can open models take? We’re entering the decisive era. This is one of the most packed recaps of open models we’ve ever had, we’re excited! Our Picks Inkling by thinkingmachines : The first model from Thinking Machines is a 975B-A41B multimodal MoE that supports text, images, and audio as inputs and produces text as output. While it is not the strongest model among peers (in China) in its size class, it is positioned to be a great base for fine-tuning, e.g., through their commercial offering, Tinker. They also release a smaller version (276B-A12B), which is really competitive for its size. Hy3 by tencent : A 295B-A21B MoE from Tencent. It improves over its predecessor across all metrics. Most notable, however, is the license change: While the previous version (covered in Artifacts 21 ) used a custom and rather restrictive license, Tencent switched to Apache 2 for this release. The model was also able to proof a 50 year old math problem (with a dedicated harness and Sol as a judge, although it is unclear how important the latter really is). Laguna-S-2.1 by poolside : Poolside quickly rose out of nowhere to become a frequent guest at Artifacts, marking its third appearance in three consecutive months. S2.1 is a newly pre- and post-trained version of the 118B-A8B MoE that fits on a DGX Spark, which brought it a lot of attention. Poolside also adopted the OpenMDW license, which is an Apache 2.0-like free license but has better legal backing for AI models specifically. The company also goes into more detail in its blog , which includes all the evaluation trajectories . This is a lot of transparency for an open model release! DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 by deepseek-ai : Just one day after OpenAI has dropped the prices of their smallest model by 80% , the whale dropped an update to their V4 Flash model, beating Luna at the pareto frontier. The bigger model is not updated yet, so it remains to be seen where it will land in terms of performance. For the initial V4 releases, the Flash version was the star of the show in terms of performance per parameter, while Pro was rather underwhelming. Kimi-K3 by moonshotai : This is the biggest open model release in some time, and we covered it in a separate post and a podcast episode . It was released under a noncommercial license, requiring inference and fine-tuning providers to enter into a commercial agreement. Kevin Xu and Graham Webster argue in a post that these licenses enable potential future government action against US entities doing business with Chinese AI companies: But if a US company needs a contract with Moonshot to provide the inference tokens that Kimi K3 generates, the picture looks different. Some of the policy tools US officials and others have debated as potential levers to restrict Chinese open model use would more clearly apply. Models General Purpose LongCat-2.0 by meituan-longcat : The Chinese DoorDash is back again. This time, the company released another big MoE with 1.6T parameters. While the model itself is not the most capable for its size beyond benchmarks, it was trained entirely on Ascend 910s, making it the first non-Huawei, non-toy model trained entirely on Chinese accelerators. Other Chinese chips are mostly used for inference (if at all). Laguna-XS-2.1 by poolside : An update to the small (33B-A3B) MoE from Poolside. Motif-3-Beta by Motif-Technologies : A preview of a 314B-A13B MoE by the Korean Motif. This is by far the company’s most ambitious model, as it is considerably larger and introduces some architectural innovations like GDLA and mHC. Apertus-v1.5-70B by swiss-ai : A continued pre-train of the fully open-source Apertus 1.0, using 2T more tokens. Instella-MoE-16B-A3B-Think by amd : A 16B-A3B MoE trained by AMD on Instinct cards. AMD also provides all the different stages, from the base to the SFT checkpoints, as well as MidTrain and DPO . Read more

The system improved scores by up to 8.3 percentage points across two benchmarks. items.title: Analyzing Financial Trends: Kalman Filtering for Gold vs Bitcoin
items.summary:
[This article was first published on DataGeeek , and kindly contributed to R-bloggers ].  (You can report issue about the content on this page here ) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't. In their paper “A Synchronized Multi‑IMU Wearable System for Tracking of Joint‑Angles in Sports Motion Analysis” ( arXiv:2607.26027v1 ), Samarasekera and colleagues set out to solve a very practical problem: how to reliably measure joint angles in dynamic sports movements using wearable IMUs . Their goal was to design a synchronized pipeline that could filter out noise, correct drift, and normalize ranges so that biomechanical signals could be trusted in real‑world conditions. Our goal is different but conceptually parallel: to apply the same pipeline logic to financial time‑series data . Instead of knee flexion angles, we analyze the comparative dynamics of Gold and Bitcoin. The challenge is similar — financial returns are noisy, prone to drift, and difficult to compare directly. By adapting their pipeline, we aim to extract latent trends, mitigate drift, normalize ranges, and highlight relative divergence between assets. The pipeline consists of four sequential stages: Indirect Kalman Filtering (IKF) – extracting latent trends from noisy log returns. State equation: x t = F ⋅ x t − 1 + w t , w t ∼ N ( 0 , Q ) Observation equation: y t = H ⋅ x t + v t , v t ∼ N ( 0 , R ) IKF separates signal from noise, with Q and R learned via maximum likelihood. Drift Mitigation via High‑Pass Filtering – removing low‑frequency bias. High‑pass operator: x t H P = x t − 1 N ∑ i = 1 N x t − i This ensures long‑term drift does not dominate short‑term dynamics. Range Normalization – mapping filtered values into a comparable scale. Normalization function: z t = x t H P − min ⁡ ( x H P ) max ⁡ ( x H P ) − min ⁡ ( x H P ) ⋅ 100 This allows Gold and Bitcoin to be compared on the same 0–100 scale. Relative Notation (Directional Divergence) – highlighting when assets move in opposite directions. Divergence indicator: D t = sign ( r t G o l d ) ≠ sign ( r t B T C ) If true, shaded regions show divergence; if false, alignment. Why This Matters For the biomechanics researchers, the pipeline meant trustworthy joint‑angle tracking . For us, the same architecture means trustworthy comparative trend analysis between financial assets. In both cases, the pipeline’s strength lies in its modularity: IKF for latent signal extraction, high‑pass filtering for drift control, normalization for comparability, and relative notation for divergence detection. ✦ R Packages in Our Pipeline To make this pipeline reproducible and transparent, we rely on a set of R packages. Each package plays a specific role in the architecture: tidyverse Purpose: Data manipulation and wrangling. Functions: mutate , rename , inner_join , drop_na . Why: Provides a clean grammar for transforming raw financial data into structured time‑series. tidyquant Purpose: Financial data acquisition and transformation. Functions: tq_get (download asset prices), tq_transmute (compute log returns). Why: Bridges tidyverse with financial APIs, enabling reproducible market data pipelines. KFAS Purpose: State‑space modeling and Kalman filtering. Functions: SSModel (define state‑space model), fitSSM (MLE parameter estimation), KFS (Kalman smoothing). Why: Implements the mathematical backbone of IKF, separating latent trends from noise. zoo Purpose: Rolling window operations. Functions: rollmean . Why: Used for high‑pass filtering by subtracting rolling averages, mitigating drift. scales Purpose: Normalization and rescaling. Functions: rescale . Why: Maps filtered trends into a 0–100 range, enabling comparability across assets. ggbraid Purpose: Divergence visualization. Functions: geom_braid . Why: Highlights periods of divergence between Gold and Bitcoin with shaded regions. ggplot2 (via tidyverse) Purpose: Visualization. Functions: geom_line , labs , theme_classic . Why: Provides the plotting framework for presenting normalized high‑pass Kalman trends. library(tidyverse)
library(tidyquant)
library(KFAS)
library(ggbraid)

# --- Step 1: Log returns ---
gold <- tq_get("GC=F", from = "2024-01-01") %>%
  tq_transmute(select = close,
               mutate_fun = periodReturn,
               period = "daily",
               type = "log")

btc <- tq_get("BTC-USD", from = "2024-01-01") %>%
  tq_transmute(select = close,
               mutate_fun = periodReturn,
               period = "daily",
               type = "log")

df <- gold %>%
  rename(ret_gold = daily.returns) %>%
  inner_join(btc %>% rename(ret_btc = daily.returns), by="date") %>%
  drop_na()

# --- Step 2: IKF (Kalman filter) ---
model_gold <- SSModel(df$ret_gold ~ SSMtrend(1, Q = list(NA)), H = NA)
model_btc  <- SSModel(df$ret_btc  ~ SSMtrend(1, Q = list(NA)), H = NA)

fit_gold <- fitSSM(model_gold, inits = c(log(var(df$ret_gold)), log(var(df$ret_gold))))
fit_btc  <- fitSSM(model_btc,  inits = c(log(var(df$ret_btc)),  log(var(df$ret_btc))))

kf_gold <- KFS(fit_gold$model, smoothing = c("state"))
kf_btc  <- KFS(fit_btc$model,  smoothing = c("state"))

trend_gold <- as.numeric(kf_gold$alphahat)
trend_btc  <- as.numeric(kf_btc$alphahat)

# --- Step 3: High-pass filter (remove low-frequency drift) ---
hp_gold <- trend_gold - zoo::rollmean(trend_gold, k=30, fill=NA, align="right")
hp_btc  <- trend_btc  - zoo::rollmean(trend_btc,  k=30, fill=NA, align="right")

# --- Step 4: Range normalization ---
gold_norm <- scales::rescale(hp_gold, to=c(0,100))
btc_norm  <- scales::rescale(hp_btc,  to=c(0,100))

# --- Step 5: Relative notation (directional divergence) ---
df_norm <- df %>%
  mutate(
    gold_norm = gold_norm,
    btc_norm  = btc_norm,
    sign_gold = sign(ret_gold),
    sign_btc  = sign(ret_btc),
    divergence = sign_gold != sign_btc
  )

# --- Plot ---
ggplot(df_norm, aes(x=date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y=gold_norm, color="Gold"), linewidth=1.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y=btc_norm, color="Bitcoin"), linewidth=1.2) +
  geom_braid(aes(ymin=gold_norm, ymax=btc_norm, fill=divergence), alpha=0.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("Gold"="#FFD700", "Bitcoin"="#1E3A8A"),
                     name = "") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("TRUE"="#FF4C4C", "FALSE"="#87CEFA"),
                    name = "Divergence") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,100)) +
  labs(title="Gold vs Bitcoin: Kalman-Filtered High-Pass Trends",
       subtitle="Directional divergence highlighted with shaded regions",
       x="", y="Normalized High-Pass Kalman Trend") +
  theme_classic(base_family = "Roboto Slab") +
  theme(
    legend.position="bottom",
    legend.title=element_text(size=12, face="bold"),
    legend.text=element_text(size=10),
    plot.title=element_text(size=16, face="bold"),
    plot.subtitle=element_text(size=12),
    axis.title=element_text(size=12, face="bold"),
    axis.text=element_text(size=10),
    panel.grid.minor=element_blank()
  ) Conclusion By adapting the IKF pipeline from the sports biomechanics paper, we demonstrate how state‑space filtering , drift mitigation, and normalization can reveal comparative dynamics among financial assets. This modular approach is reproducible and extensible to other domains where latent trends and divergence matter. [This article was first published on DataGeeek, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

In their paper “A Synchronized Multi‑IMU Wearable System for Tracking of Joint‑Angles in Sports Motion Analysis” (arXiv:2607.26027v1), Samarasekera and colleagues set out to solve a very practical problem: how to reliably measure joint angles in dynamic sports movements using wearable IMUs. Their goal was to design a synchronized pipeline that could filter out noise, correct drift, and normalize ranges so that biomechanical signals could be trusted in real‑world conditions.

Our goal is different but conceptually parallel: to apply the same pipeline logic to financial time‑series data. Instead of knee flexion angles, we analyze the comparative dynamics of Gold and Bitcoin. The challenge is similar — financial returns are noisy, prone to drift, and difficult to compare directly. By adapting their pipeline, we aim to extract latent trends, mitigate drift, normalize ranges, and highlight relative divergence between assets.

The pipeline consists of four sequential stages:

  1. Indirect Kalman Filtering (IKF) – extracting latent trends from noisy log returns.
    • State equation:

xt=F⋅xt−1+wt,wt∼N(0,Q)

  • Observation equation:

yt=H⋅xt+vt,vt∼N(0,R)

  • IKF separates signal from noise, with Q and R learned via maximum likelihood.
  1. Drift Mitigation via High‑Pass Filtering – removing low‑frequency bias.
    • High‑pass operator:

xtHP=xt−1N∑i=1Nxt−i

  • This ensures long‑term drift does not dominate short‑term dynamics.
  1. Range Normalization – mapping filtered values into a comparable scale.
    • Normalization function:

zt=xtHP−min⁡(xHP)max⁡(xHP)−min⁡(xHP)⋅100

  • This allows Gold and Bitcoin to be compared on the same 0–100 scale.
  1. Relative Notation (Directional Divergence) – highlighting when assets move in opposite directions.
    • Divergence indicator:

Dt=sign(rtGold)≠sign(rtBTC)

  • If true, shaded regions show divergence; if false, alignment.
Why This Matters
  • For the biomechanics researchers, the pipeline meant trustworthy joint‑angle tracking.
  • For us, the same architecture means trustworthy comparative trend analysis between financial assets.
  • In both cases, the pipeline’s strength lies in its modularity: IKF for latent signal extraction, high‑pass filtering for drift control, normalization for comparability, and relative notation for divergence detection.
✦ R Packages in Our Pipeline

To make this pipeline reproducible and transparent, we rely on a set of R packages. Each package plays a specific role in the architecture:

  1. tidyverse
    • Purpose: Data manipulation and wrangling.
    • Functions: mutate, rename, inner_join, drop_na.
    • Why: Provides a clean grammar for transforming raw financial data into structured time‑series.
  2. tidyquant
    • Purpose: Financial data acquisition and transformation.
    • Functions: tq_get (download asset prices), tq_transmute (compute log returns).
    • Why: Bridges tidyverse with financial APIs, enabling reproducible market data pipelines.
  3. KFAS
    • Purpose: State‑space modeling and Kalman filtering.
    • Functions: SSModel (define state‑space model), fitSSM (MLE parameter estimation), KFS (Kalman smoothing).
    • Why: Implements the mathematical backbone of IKF, separating latent trends from noise.
  4. zoo
    • Purpose: Rolling window operations.
    • Functions: rollmean.
    • Why: Used for high‑pass filtering by subtracting rolling averages, mitigating drift.
  5. scales
    • Purpose: Normalization and rescaling.
    • Functions: rescale.
    • Why: Maps filtered trends into a 0–100 range, enabling comparability across assets.
  6. ggbraid
    • Purpose: Divergence visualization.
    • Functions: geom_braid.
    • Why: Highlights periods of divergence between Gold and Bitcoin with shaded regions.
  7. ggplot2 (via tidyverse)
    • Purpose: Visualization.
    • Functions: geom_line, labs, theme_classic.
    • Why: Provides the plotting framework for presenting normalized high‑pass Kalman trends.
library(tidyverse)
library(tidyquant)
library(KFAS)
library(ggbraid)

# --- Step 1: Log returns ---
gold <- tq_get("GC=F", from = "2024-01-01") %>%
  tq_transmute(select = close,
               mutate_fun = periodReturn,
               period = "daily",
               type = "log")

btc <- tq_get("BTC-USD", from = "2024-01-01") %>%
  tq_transmute(select = close,
               mutate_fun = periodReturn,
               period = "daily",
               type = "log")

df <- gold %>%
  rename(ret_gold = daily.returns) %>%
  inner_join(btc %>% rename(ret_btc = daily.returns), by="date") %>%
  drop_na()

# --- Step 2: IKF (Kalman filter) ---
model_gold <- SSModel(df$ret_gold ~ SSMtrend(1, Q = list(NA)), H = NA)
model_btc  <- SSModel(df$ret_btc  ~ SSMtrend(1, Q = list(NA)), H = NA)

fit_gold <- fitSSM(model_gold, inits = c(log(var(df$ret_gold)), log(var(df$ret_gold))))
fit_btc  <- fitSSM(model_btc,  inits = c(log(var(df$ret_btc)),  log(var(df$ret_btc))))

kf_gold <- KFS(fit_gold$model, smoothing = c("state"))
kf_btc  <- KFS(fit_btc$model,  smoothing = c("state"))

trend_gold <- as.numeric(kf_gold$alphahat)
trend_btc  <- as.numeric(kf_btc$alphahat)

# --- Step 3: High-pass filter (remove low-frequency drift) ---
hp_gold <- trend_gold - zoo::rollmean(trend_gold, k=30, fill=NA, align="right")
hp_btc  <- trend_btc  - zoo::rollmean(trend_btc,  k=30, fill=NA, align="right")

# --- Step 4: Range normalization ---
gold_norm <- scales::rescale(hp_gold, to=c(0,100))
btc_norm  <- scales::rescale(hp_btc,  to=c(0,100))

# --- Step 5: Relative notation (directional divergence) ---
df_norm <- df %>%
  mutate(
    gold_norm = gold_norm,
    btc_norm  = btc_norm,
    sign_gold = sign(ret_gold),
    sign_btc  = sign(ret_btc),
    divergence = sign_gold != sign_btc
  )

# --- Plot ---
ggplot(df_norm, aes(x=date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y=gold_norm, color="Gold"), linewidth=1.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y=btc_norm, color="Bitcoin"), linewidth=1.2) +
  geom_braid(aes(ymin=gold_norm, ymax=btc_norm, fill=divergence), alpha=0.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("Gold"="#FFD700", "Bitcoin"="#1E3A8A"),
                     name = "") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("TRUE"="#FF4C4C", "FALSE"="#87CEFA"),
                    name = "Divergence") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,100)) +
  labs(title="Gold vs Bitcoin: Kalman-Filtered High-Pass Trends",
       subtitle="Directional divergence highlighted with shaded regions",
       x="", y="Normalized High-Pass Kalman Trend") +
  theme_classic(base_family = "Roboto Slab") +
  theme(
    legend.position="bottom",
    legend.title=element_text(size=12, face="bold"),
    legend.text=element_text(size=10),
    plot.title=element_text(size=16, face="bold"),
    plot.subtitle=element_text(size=12),
    axis.title=element_text(size=12, face="bold"),
    axis.text=element_text(size=10),
    panel.grid.minor=element_blank()
  )
Conclusion

By adapting the IKF pipeline from the sports biomechanics paper, we demonstrate how state‑space filtering, drift mitigation, and normalization can reveal comparative dynamics among financial assets. This modular approach is reproducible and extensible to other domains where latent trends and divergence matter.

items.title: A real macOS flaw worth $200K went unreported because Apple's bug bounty inbox was full of AI slop
items.summary: Apple's bug bounty program is drowning in AI-generated bug reports. The company has capped submissions per researcher because fabricated reports are clogging the review pipeline. As a result, Italian startup Bynario was initially unable to report a serious macOS vulnerability worth up to $200,000 on the black market. items.title: I ate at Gordon Ramsay, Lisa Vanderpump, and Giada De Laurentiis' Las Vegas restaurants. One got every dish right.
items.summary: I tried Giada De Laurentiis, Gordon Ramsay, and Lisa Vanderpump's Las Vegas restaurants. Jacob Kepler for BI I compared Las Vegas restaurants owned by Gordon Ramsay, Lisa Vanderpump, and Giada De Laurentiis. Vanderpump has wild cocktails, while De Laurentiis sticks to Italian-American classics. My favorite was Ramsay's Hell's Kitchen restaurant, where every dish was perfectly executed. Trips to Las Vegas have started to look a little different since I entered my 30s. Gone are the days when my friends and I would solely survive on McDonald's or Panda Express, lugging grease-stained brown bags or heaving cartons of orange chicken as we rushed from the pool party to the nightclub. Oh, to be young. Or at least that young! I'm still going to the clubs, but you won't catch me at the Venetian food court anymore. Dining in Sin City has never been better, and I treat each visit as an opportunity to explore. On my most recent Vegas trip to review The Vanderpump Hotel , I got the chance to try three very different restaurants by three very big names: Lisa Vanderpump, Gordon Ramsay , and Giada De Laurentiis . There were highs, there were lows, there were cocktails covered in smoke. There were birdcages stuffed with charcuterie, towers stacked with crostini and crepes, and who could forget the world's most famous beef Wellington ? Here's how it all went. My first meal of the trip was lunch at Giada, located at the brand-new Vanderpump Hotel. Jacob Kepler for BI Giada was De Laurentiis' very first restaurant, opening at The Cromwell hotel in the heart of the Las Vegas Strip in June 2014. The property has since been completely revamped by Vanderpump and now bears her name, but Giada remains in the same space. When I walked into the restaurant, something about the interior design felt distinctly '90s. Jacob Kepler for BI The nearly orange glow of the lighting and the multicolored patterns on the chairs made me feel like I was back in a quirky coffee shop from my childhood. Waiting on each marble table were red water glasses decorated with stars and salmon-pink cloth napkins. My friend Kayla and I sat down in a comfy crescent-shaped booth that faced the floor-to-ceiling windows, offering front-row seats to the Strip. Our server said the view was even better at night, when everything was lit up and you could watch the Fountains of Bellagio. We decided to start with the $40 Brunch Favorites Tower. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider We loved the crostini, which arrived in thin logs with a generous piping of ricotta on top. The cheese was lightly kissed with truffle and hot honey, creating a sweet-and-savory bite that felt indulgent. The crepes — which came with either Nutella and strawberry or smoked salmon and caviar — were less impressive. The savory crepe was surprisingly bland, and we couldn't taste any of the caviar. The bacon-wrapped dates at the bottom of the tower were a bit heavy, but the creamy gorgonzola dipping crema added some balance. Next up was the chopped Italian salad. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider We figured we needed some balance before a round of pasta, but the chopped salad was lacking in ingredients and flavor. There wasn't enough salami or baby tomatoes, and, overall, everything needed a big punch of salt. I tried a couple of additional Giada appetizers while getting room service at The Vanderpump Hotel and would recommend the (really delicious) $17 orzo meatballs or $34 salumi and formaggi dish instead. We tried the breakfast risotto, rigatoni alla vodka, and cavatelli pasta for our entrées. Jacob Kepler for BI The star of the trio was the $22 rigatoni alla vodka, which features pomodoro, a dollop of ricotta, and basil. The noodles, covered in sauce and dusted in cheese, looked beautiful on the plate. Each bite was satisfyingly creamy and rich, with a hint of sweetness. We also liked the breakfast risotto, a fun Italian-American fusion breakfast that featured sunny-side-up eggs, applewood-smoked bacon, and sugar snap peas. It wasn't the most memorable dish, but the risotto was cooked well, and I liked the extra crunch from the peas and bacon. Our least favorite dish of the day was the $25 cavatelli. We ordered the pasta since it uses the same lemon crema as the signature lemon spaghetti on Giada's dinner menu, but we could barely taste any lemon. The shrimp on top was dry and looked unappetizing against the pale cavatelli, which had been topped with crispy capers. Nothing about the dish seemed to work. A Caesars representative declined to comment on the food at Giada. The next day, we headed across the street to Caesars Palace for lunch at Hell's Kitchen. Hell's Kitchen at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas. Courtesy of Caesars Entertainment Although I've never seen "Hell's Kitchen," which is now in its 25th season, I'm a huge fan of Gordon Ramsay. I've been to a number of his restaurants in London — including his very fun bottomless pizza spot — and love whipping up his recipes at home (my favorite is his 15-minute Bolognese ). So I was super excited to finally dine at one of his Hell's Kitchen restaurants , all of which serve his signature beef Wellington dish. The restaurant's interior is designed to make guests feel as if they're on the show's set. Hell's Kitchen design was inspired by the set of Ramsay's show. Courtesy of Caesars Entertainment The Hell's Kitchen restaurant features a massive open kitchen split into a red and blue side, with chefs wearing either red or blue bandanas to signify their team — just like on the show. Dangling from the ceiling are dozens of light fixtures shaped like golden pitchforks, part of the series' iconic logo. We decided to start our day with cocktails that we could eat and drink. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider There's nothing like a good Bloody Mary — or in this case, the Hell's Mary — to start your day in Vegas. Hell's Kitchen's $25 version includes Absolut Tabasco vodka mixed with a tomato-spice blend and a smoked paprika rim. It was one of the best Bloody Marys I've had in a long time, refreshing while still packing a spicy punch. The $24 shrimp cocktail was pretty pricey for four shrimp, but they were extremely plump and fresh — clearly high-quality. The bright and tangy gin cocktail sauce was so delicious, we swept up every last drop. Next up were the pan-seared scallops. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider As someone who watches a lot of cooking competitions, I know how tricky scallops can be. I also learned that they're a frequent challenge on "Hell's Kitchen," with Ramsay known to scream "IT'S RAW" to anyone who dares undercook the pesky bivalve. There was no such mistake during our lunch. The scallops, perched in a lovely citrus beurre blanc, were butter-soft. The bacon lardons provided some smoky crunch against their tender sweetness, and the English pea purée added a beautiful burst of color. I couldn't resist trying the onion soup. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider If you've read any of my cooking articles, you'll know that I'm a massive soup fan . I'm in a group chat dedicated to sharing pictures and soup recipes (shout-out to my "soup girlz"), and I make a massive batch of homemade chicken stock at least once a year. So the 110-degree Vegas heat did not dissuade me from trying Ramsay's $19 onion soup. And I'm so glad, because this dish truly felt gourmet. Mixed with lobster, black truffle, and potato hash, each sip was creamy and decadent. I would definitely order it again. The beef Wellington lived up to its hype. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Every famous chef has their iconic dish. For Julia Child, it was beef bourguignon . For Wolfgang Puck, it's the smoked salmon pizza . And for Ramsay, it's beef Wellington. While I've dined at a handful of Ramsay's restaurants, this was the first time I got to see his legendary recipe up close. The puff pastry that encased the beef had been baked to a beautiful caramel color, while the medium-rare filet glowed pink. Tucked into the accompanying potato purée was a pool of red-wine demi-glace, presented without a drop out of place. It was a beautiful plate. And just like every other dish at Hell's Kitchen, the $73.95 beef Wellington was excellent. The puff pastry was flaky and warm, hugging the tender beef inside. I'd run each piece through the velvety potatoes for the perfect comforting bite. The flavors immediately brought me back to the Sunday roast dinners I'd eat while living in London. We capped off our meal with the $15.95 sticky toffee pudding, which I highly recommend. It was the exact amount of sweetness we needed after such a big lunch. For our last dinner in Vegas, we decided to travel to Vanderpump's Parisian escape — no passport required. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider In addition to her hotel, Vanderpump has four restaurants and bars in Vegas: Pinky's at the Flamingo, Vanderpump à Paris at Paris Las Vegas, Vanderpump Cocktail Garden at Caesars Palace , and Gigolo at The Vanderpump Hotel. I tried all four places during my recent trip , going on my own Vanderpump Vegas crawl. Vanderpump à Paris was one of my favorite spots thanks to its stunning decor, imaginative cocktails, and a delicious spread of carbs. Vanderpump à Paris is designed to evoke a rainy night in the City of Light. Inside Vanderpump à Paris at the Paris Las Vegas hotel. Ernesto Garrido We strolled beneath the restaurant's high stone archways and were transported into a moody, romantic space that felt worlds away from the nearby slot machines. The dim lighting and velvet purple booths made the restaurant feel cozy, while the chandeliers, marble tables, and fountains added drama and elegance. Behind the marble bar, you'll find a fake window, designed to look like raindrops on glass. Stare long enough, and you'll notice the Eiffel Tower winking back. After ordering a round of espresso martinis, we dug into our first app. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I love a good charcuterie board, so I couldn't resist trying Vanderpump's $45 Birdcage Á Charcuterie. The meats — including salami, capocollo, and mini baguette rosettes, a traditional French sandwich — were all delicious, and I loved the housemade potato chips, which were crisped to perfection. My one wish was that they had a creamy dipping sauce to offset that salty crunch. The birdcage comes with a sharp mustard for the meat, but it didn't pair well with the chips. Vanderpump has a fantastic Boursin dip at Gigolo that would be perfect for them. The $30 Truffle-Stuffed Vanderpump Baguette was my favorite dish of the night. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I wasn't planning to dig into a baguette covered with black summer truffles and triple crème Brie before a long night out in Vegas, but, honestly, I have no regrets. The golden baguette had a lovely crust that wasn't too crunchy, giving way to the ultra-creamy cheese. And the truffle honey added extra umami — it all tasted so decadent! I have thought about this baguette a lot since leaving Vegas. And the Louvre at First Sight was the best cocktail of my entire trip. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Only the garnish of my $27 drink was visible at first, peeking through a miniature Louvre pyramid filled with smoke. Tendrils were already seeping from the base, turning the dinner table into our own little club. A cloud of smoke escaped as the server lifted the case, revealing the pink mezcal cocktail sitting atop fresh flower petals. The drink was both smoky and sweet, with a lovely freshness from the prickly pear and a kick of jalapeño honey. It went down easily (and quickly). We also tried the $50 Lovelocked, which comes with two cocktails, plus a padlock, key, and marker. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider The drink was inspired by Paris' former Love Lock Bridge, which nearly sank from the weight of one million tourists' pledges of love. Now you can re-create the moment at Vanderpump's "Wall of Love." The concept was cute, but I didn't love the gin and hibiscus drink as much as the Louvre at First Sight, which provided more flavor and drama at a lower price. The $23 Mini Monsieurs were delicious, but I wouldn't recommend ordering them alongside the baguette. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I ordered our entrées after a few cocktails, which is probably why I decided on sandwiches stuffed with Gruyère and covered in béchamel, along with a $17 tub of Gruyère frites. If I'm having more than one drink, an order of fries is almost guaranteed. The frites were deliciously seasoned, and the Mini Monsieurs were a cheesy dream. But overall, there were too many carbs for one meal, a fault of my own ordering! We were completely stuffed, but when the waiter asked if we wanted dessert, how could we say no? The $16 Rose & Rosé Eclairs are light, bite-sized, and a nice little treat to end the night. There was never a dull moment during my Vegas feast, but there was a clear favorite. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider From the cocktails to the dessert, every dish at Hell's Kitchen was perfectly executed. If this were a competition, Ramsay would have won easily. But that's not to say I wouldn't go back to Vanderpump à Paris for another smoking cocktail and truffle-stuffed baguette. And if you're staying at The Vanderpump Hotel, I highly recommend ordering Giada's orzo meatballs and the salumi and formaggi plate for room service. The best part about Vegas is that there's truly something for every mood at every hour — even a 40-piece chicken-nugget box, if that's what your young heart desires. Read the original article on Business Insider

There was no such mistake during our lunch. The scallops, perched in a lovely citrus beurre blanc, were butter-soft. The bacon lardons provided some smoky crunch against their tender sweetness, and the English pea purée added a beautiful burst of color.

I couldn't resist trying the onion soup.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

If you've read any of my cooking articles, you'll know that I'm a massive soup fan. I'm in a group chat dedicated to sharing pictures and soup recipes (shout-out to my "soup girlz"), and I make a massive batch of homemade chicken stock at least once a year. So the 110-degree Vegas heat did not dissuade me from trying Ramsay's $19 onion soup.

And I'm so glad, because this dish truly felt gourmet. Mixed with lobster, black truffle, and potato hash, each sip was creamy and decadent. I would definitely order it again.

The beef Wellington lived up to its hype.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

Every famous chef has their iconic dish. For Julia Child, it was beef bourguignon. For Wolfgang Puck, it's the smoked salmon pizza. And for Ramsay, it's beef Wellington.

While I've dined at a handful of Ramsay's restaurants, this was the first time I got to see his legendary recipe up close. The puff pastry that encased the beef had been baked to a beautiful caramel color, while the medium-rare filet glowed pink. Tucked into the accompanying potato purée was a pool of red-wine demi-glace, presented without a drop out of place. It was a beautiful plate.

And just like every other dish at Hell's Kitchen, the $73.95 beef Wellington was excellent. The puff pastry was flaky and warm, hugging the tender beef inside. I'd run each piece through the velvety potatoes for the perfect comforting bite. The flavors immediately brought me back to the Sunday roast dinners I'd eat while living in London.

We capped off our meal with the $15.95 sticky toffee pudding, which I highly recommend. It was the exact amount of sweetness we needed after such a big lunch.

For our last dinner in Vegas, we decided to travel to Vanderpump's Parisian escape — no passport required.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

In addition to her hotel, Vanderpump has four restaurants and bars in Vegas: Pinky's at the Flamingo, Vanderpump à Paris at Paris Las Vegas, Vanderpump Cocktail Garden at Caesars Palace, and Gigolo at The Vanderpump Hotel.

I tried all four places during my recent trip, going on my own Vanderpump Vegas crawl. Vanderpump à Paris was one of my favorite spots thanks to its stunning decor, imaginative cocktails, and a delicious spread of carbs.

Vanderpump à Paris is designed to evoke a rainy night in the City of Light.
Inside Vanderpump à Paris at the Paris Las Vegas hotel.

Ernesto Garrido

We strolled beneath the restaurant's high stone archways and were transported into a moody, romantic space that felt worlds away from the nearby slot machines. The dim lighting and velvet purple booths made the restaurant feel cozy, while the chandeliers, marble tables, and fountains added drama and elegance.

Behind the marble bar, you'll find a fake window, designed to look like raindrops on glass. Stare long enough, and you'll notice the Eiffel Tower winking back.

After ordering a round of espresso martinis, we dug into our first app.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

I love a good charcuterie board, so I couldn't resist trying Vanderpump's $45 Birdcage Á Charcuterie.

The meats — including salami, capocollo, and mini baguette rosettes, a traditional French sandwich — were all delicious, and I loved the housemade potato chips, which were crisped to perfection. My one wish was that they had a creamy dipping sauce to offset that salty crunch. The birdcage comes with a sharp mustard for the meat, but it didn't pair well with the chips. Vanderpump has a fantastic Boursin dip at Gigolo that would be perfect for them.

The $30 Truffle-Stuffed Vanderpump Baguette was my favorite dish of the night.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

I wasn't planning to dig into a baguette covered with black summer truffles and triple crème Brie before a long night out in Vegas, but, honestly, I have no regrets.

The golden baguette had a lovely crust that wasn't too crunchy, giving way to the ultra-creamy cheese. And the truffle honey added extra umami — it all tasted so decadent! I have thought about this baguette a lot since leaving Vegas.

And the Louvre at First Sight was the best cocktail of my entire trip.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

Only the garnish of my $27 drink was visible at first, peeking through a miniature Louvre pyramid filled with smoke. Tendrils were already seeping from the base, turning the dinner table into our own little club.

A cloud of smoke escaped as the server lifted the case, revealing the pink mezcal cocktail sitting atop fresh flower petals. The drink was both smoky and sweet, with a lovely freshness from the prickly pear and a kick of jalapeño honey. It went down easily (and quickly).

We also tried the $50 Lovelocked, which comes with two cocktails, plus a padlock, key, and marker.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

The drink was inspired by Paris' former Love Lock Bridge, which nearly sank from the weight of one million tourists' pledges of love. Now you can re-create the moment at Vanderpump's "Wall of Love."

The concept was cute, but I didn't love the gin and hibiscus drink as much as the Louvre at First Sight, which provided more flavor and drama at a lower price.

The $23 Mini Monsieurs were delicious, but I wouldn't recommend ordering them alongside the baguette.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

I ordered our entrées after a few cocktails, which is probably why I decided on sandwiches stuffed with Gruyère and covered in béchamel, along with a $17 tub of Gruyère frites. If I'm having more than one drink, an order of fries is almost guaranteed.

The frites were deliciously seasoned, and the Mini Monsieurs were a cheesy dream. But overall, there were too many carbs for one meal, a fault of my own ordering!

We were completely stuffed, but when the waiter asked if we wanted dessert, how could we say no? The $16 Rose & Rosé Eclairs are light, bite-sized, and a nice little treat to end the night.

There was never a dull moment during my Vegas feast, but there was a clear favorite.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

From the cocktails to the dessert, every dish at Hell's Kitchen was perfectly executed. If this were a competition, Ramsay would have won easily.

But that's not to say I wouldn't go back to Vanderpump à Paris for another smoking cocktail and truffle-stuffed baguette. And if you're staying at The Vanderpump Hotel, I highly recommend ordering Giada's orzo meatballs and the salumi and formaggi plate for room service.

The best part about Vegas is that there's truly something for every mood at every hour — even a 40-piece chicken-nugget box, if that's what your young heart desires.

items.title: I'm in my 50s, can't find a job, and am already draining my 401k. I've never felt closer to failure.
items.summary: Laura Lynch is taking a coding course and leaning on family to get by. Olga Pankova/Getty Images Laura Lynch was laid off from her middle manager role in 2025 and has struggled to find work since. She's eating into her 401K and considering downsizing while skill-building to create opportunities. Lynch says her daily struggle is giving into feelings of failure. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Laura Vandemark Lynch, in her 50s, based in Long Island, New York. I was an office manager for a multi-specialty healthcare provider for two and a half years. Then, in March 2025, the company reorganized and let several middle managers go, including me. It was shocking because I felt like I had done so much in that particular office. But to be honest, while I was upset about my job being terminated, I was also relieved. As a person in my late 50s working mostly with younger people, it felt like there were a lot of them trying to mold me into what they wanted. I've struggled to find a job since then. This is the first time in my life that I don't know that I'll have a happy ending. In Still in the Game , Business Insider is chronicling the realities of job hunting in your 50s — from overcoming age bias and navigating career transitions to rebuilding confidence, updating skills, and finding new opportunities in a competitive job market. Read more stories here , and share your own experience here . I know I'll be OK, but that might mean my husband and I moving in with my mother, selling our house, or draining my 401(k). It feels like I am standing on the precipice of failure, and it's an uncomfortable place to be, but it's not over. Here's what I'm doing to get by. I'm learning new skills to create more job opportunities When I first started applying to jobs, I was looking exclusively for in-person jobs because my role in operations management in healthcare requires me to be at the facility where I work. I've found that many organizations are eliminating middle management roles , making it harder to find jobs that use my skill set, so I've started applying to remote roles as well on job boards and directly through company websites. I'm trying to diversify my skills, so I'm taking a coding in healthcare course. It was a part of my most recent job that I enjoyed a lot. It's not patient-facing, meaning it's not necessarily a job that requires me to be in a hospital or even in person. That allows me to look into remote opportunities and office job opportunities. I'm digging into my 401k I'm now eating into my 401(k) , and I don't know what to do. My husband works, but losing my salary has been financially devastating. I'm wondering whether we should move somewhere else that's less expensive, but I don't know what's best. My mom has been really supportive, and my husband has helped me look for jobs. He knows that it's not as simple as throwing my résumé online and getting jumped on to get a job. My family has stepped in to help me feel better about my situation My adult son, who lives at home, keeps trying to get me to go outside and garden, even though I have a track record of killing plants. My family is trying to help in their own way, especially by getting me out of the house. I've also been teaching my son to drive, which really gets me out of my own head. Believe it or not, they help by not pushing. They know I'm doing everything I can at this point. I feel like age is a factor, and it makes me feel invisible I feel like my age is a factor in why I've struggled to get hired, although I don't understand why. Just because I'm in my 50s doesn't mean my brain doesn't function well enough to do the job. I have a lot of life experience and can handle stressful situations. In my previous jobs, I had people who relied on me and my expertise on a daily basis to help them find solutions. I went from playing an important role — having a purpose — to feeling like nothing. It feels like being in the sixth grade and not getting chosen for dodgeball. I have days when I wonder what the point is of getting dressed, but I'm rejecting those feelings I try not to dwell on that feeling, but there are times I think about doing something like vacuuming the house, and I think, "What's the point of that, too?" It's crushing to go from being a rock for so many people to feeling irrelevant and unnecessary. My daily struggle is not to give in to the feelings of failure . To see it, own it, feel it, and then reject it. I have days when I want to give up, but I won't. If I could tell anybody else going through this situation anything, I'd say don't let this be the ending of your story. Are you navigating a career change in your 50s? This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Laura Vandemark Lynch, in her 50s, based in Long Island, New York.

I was an office manager for a multi-specialty healthcare provider for two and a half years. Then, in March 2025, the company reorganized and let several middle managers go, including me.

It was shocking because I felt like I had done so much in that particular office. But to be honest, while I was upset about my job being terminated, I was also relieved.

As a person in my late 50s working mostly with younger people, it felt like there were a lot of them trying to mold me into what they wanted.

I know I'll be OK, but that might mean my husband and I moving in with my mother, selling our house, or draining my 401(k). It feels like I am standing on the precipice of failure, and it's an uncomfortable place to be, but it's not over. Here's what I'm doing to get by.

I'm learning new skills to create more job opportunities

When I first started applying to jobs, I was looking exclusively for in-person jobs because my role in operations management in healthcare requires me to be at the facility where I work.

I've found that many organizations are eliminating middle management roles, making it harder to find jobs that use my skill set, so I've started applying to remote roles as well on job boards and directly through company websites.

I'm trying to diversify my skills, so I'm taking a coding in healthcare course. It was a part of my most recent job that I enjoyed a lot. It's not patient-facing, meaning it's not necessarily a job that requires me to be in a hospital or even in person. That allows me to look into remote opportunities and office job opportunities.

I'm digging into my 401k

I'm now eating into my 401(k), and I don't know what to do. My husband works, but losing my salary has been financially devastating.

I'm wondering whether we should move somewhere else that's less expensive, but I don't know what's best.

My mom has been really supportive, and my husband has helped me look for jobs. He knows that it's not as simple as throwing my résumé online and getting jumped on to get a job.

My adult son, who lives at home, keeps trying to get me to go outside and garden, even though I have a track record of killing plants. My family is trying to help in their own way, especially by getting me out of the house.

I've also been teaching my son to drive, which really gets me out of my own head. Believe it or not, they help by not pushing. They know I'm doing everything I can at this point.

Just because I'm in my 50s doesn't mean my brain doesn't function well enough to do the job. I have a lot of life experience and can handle stressful situations. In my previous jobs, I had people who relied on me and my expertise on a daily basis to help them find solutions. I went from playing an important role — having a purpose — to feeling like nothing.

It feels like being in the sixth grade and not getting chosen for dodgeball.

I try not to dwell on that feeling, but there are times I think about doing something like vacuuming the house, and I think, "What's the point of that, too?" It's crushing to go from being a rock for so many people to feeling irrelevant and unnecessary.

My daily struggle is not to give in to the feelings of failure. To see it, own it, feel it, and then reject it. I have days when I want to give up, but I won't. If I could tell anybody else going through this situation anything, I'd say don't let this be the ending of your story.

items.title: I'm a 76-year-old baby boomer who has kept up with technology. It's helped me grow in my career and stay relevant.
items.summary: The author is a baby boomer who chose to keep up with technology. Courtesy of Beth Sobiloff I'm a baby boomer who has kept up with technological advancements. Throughout my career, I adapted to social media, advanced cameras, and website design. I believe keeping up with tech has helped me stay relevant as a baby boomer. When I took a typing class at 14, little did I know I was building a foundation that would help me keep up with technological changes over the next several decades. After college, I spent years working as a secretary, office manager, and eventually, executive assistant . My typing skills helped, but I was also forced to grow along with technology — from manual typewriters to electric typewriters to computers. The various jobs that I held were never very fulfilling or challenging, but being a single mother with three children left me little time to make a career move. That changed when my youngest became a teenager. The World Wide Web was born In 2000, the internet was growing, and companies were starting to have their own websites to market their businesses. I took a webmaster class because it seemed like designing websites was something I would like, and that changed everything. I did well in the class, mainly because I was familiar with computer programs and how to work with them. Web development languages were not too difficult, but they pushed my technical skills to the next level. My keyboarding skills were a plus. After the class, I learned about business networking and started a freelance web design business. Tech started to change rapidly The technology behind building a website has changed drastically over the past two decades. Had I not continued to learn about and embrace new technology, I would not have been able to continue my business. These advances affected not only how a website was constructed, but also how a small-business owner marketed his/her business. Ads in the yellow pages became social media posts. It was my job to guide my clients through all of these changes so that their businesses would survive. Therefore, I was forced to learn and use them myself. Still, at times, I fought change. As cellphone technology advanced, I was determined not to start texting until I realized that my children never responded to my phone calls, only text messages. Then clients began communicating via text message, and I really had to accept that texting was here to stay. My technology skills translated from computers to cameras In 2014, when I decided to create a community television show called "Two Grannies on the Road" as a side project, new technology was once again forced upon me. I had to learn to operate new, more complex video equipment and edit the videos we created. This was a much easier process because of my web design experience. Over the past dozen years of creating videos, this technology has changed tremendously as well. Change is inevitable The lesson for me is that things are always changing, and if you're not growing, you're shrinking. I'm always advocating that baby boomers are not irrelevant. But we may appear that way to the rest of the world if we are fighting hard to keep things the same as they've always been, especially when it comes to technology. Admittedly, it gets harder to learn new things as we get older. However, that learning has been shown to help keep our minds sharp. I'm now 76, traveling around my state, and posting about my journey on social media. I wouldn't be able to do all of this if I hadn't kept up with tech. Looking back over the years, I'm very glad I chose to embrace changes in technology. Beth Sobiloff is a grandmother, web designer, knitter, and founder of the "Two Grannies on the Road." items.title: We went back to Ukraine and were stunned at how much its weapons have evolved in just one year
items.summary: Ukrainian soldiers are relying more on shotguns for last-resort drone defense. Jose Colon/Anadolu via Getty Images This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Ukraine's new generation of robotic weapons At Business Insider, we're a little obsessed with weapons and defense as part of our technology and innovation coverage. To get you the latest from the field, we sent two journalists, Robert Leslie and Jake Epstein , to Ukraine in May. Their coverage is here , and more is coming. Robert and Jake, what was the single biggest surprise from your trip? JE: For me, how much progress Ukraine has made with robotics and drones compared with my previous visit in March 2025. The tech is far more sophisticated and is increasingly reliant on AI. RL: Hearing from military units about how fast they can develop new iterations of their ground, air, and sea drones was eye-popping. In just a few weeks, they can design and battle-test technology that would take peace-time armies months, even years. How is this new tech directly supporting the human soldiers still risking their lives? JE: The best example is ground robots replacing humans in dangerous front-line missions, including retrieving wounded soldiers and transporting them to safer locations for care. RL: We also saw giant bomber drones that are increasingly being deployed as heavy-lift platforms to deliver food, medicine, and water to the front. What do you now see as the biggest questions about this war and the future of war? JE: The heavy drone saturation on the battlefield has prevented either side from capturing any meaningful territory in years. What seems more impactful now are deep strikes: for Ukraine, mid- to long-range drone attacks on Russian logistics, supply routes, and energy infrastructure. RL: The use of AI in target identification and drone navigation is widespread, but in most cases, a human hand is still on the trigger. The big question is, how soon before AI completes the "kill"? items.title: Solon.cfg() Everything: The Programmatic Config Center Behind SolonProps — Typed Getters, Prefix Groups, and Bean Binding
items.summary: Most frameworks make you read config the same way: sprinkle @Value annotations everywhere, or grab a string from Environment and parse it yourself every single time. It works, but the code ends up with a hundred tiny, untestable couplings to a file somewhere. Solon's answer is different. Config is not scattered across annotations — it lives in one place, and you can reach it from anywhere in your app. That place is SolonProps , the application's property collection (a.k.a. the config center). You grab it with a single static call: SolonProps props = Solon . cfg (); That's it. No injection, no context lookup.
